s: An archduke's island garden, five minutes by ferry
w: Five minutes off the Old City by ferry, this small island once belonged to Archduke Maximilian - the Austrian who briefly ruled as Emperor of Mexico. His monastery and botanical garden still survive. Above them, a French Napoleonic fort crowns the island's high point, later renamed Maximilian's Tower in his honor.
_facts: Island 600 metres from Dubrovnik's Old City port, regular ferry service
Archduke Maximilian, later briefly Emperor of Mexico, kept a holiday home here; a monastery and botanical garden survive from his era
Fort Royal Castle at the island's highest point (96m), built by the French under Napoleon, later renamed Maximilian's Tower by the Austrians

s: One building, and the whole republic ran from it
w: For over four centuries, the government of the Republic of Ragusa answered to this one palace: the Rector's seat, the Minor Council's chamber, the state administration. It also held the armoury, the gunpowder store, the watch house and the prison - a republic's machinery under one roof.
_facts: Seat of the Rector of the Republic of Ragusa from the 14th century until 1808
Also seat of the Minor Council and the state administration
Housed an armoury, the powder magazine, the watch house and a prison

s: The fort Venice tried to build first - and lost
w: Nicknamed Dubrovnik's Gibraltar, this clifftop fortress exists because locals beat Venice to the punch: Venetian ships arrived in the 11th century loaded with materials, only to find the fort standing already, and were sent home. The Chronicles of Ragusa say it went up in three months; it now doubles as a theatre.
_facts: Fortress outside the western wall of Dubrovnik, 37 metres above sea level, known as "Dubrovnik's Gibraltar"
Early 11th century: Venice attempted to build a fort on the same spot first, but Dubrovnik's people built it first and turned the Venetian ships away
Per the Chronicles of Ragusa, built within three months; now doubles as a theatre venue for plays

s: The mountain that gave Dubrovnik its name
w: Dubrovnik takes its name from the oak forests, dubrava, once covering this mountain behind the city. A French fort crowns the 412-metre summit, now a museum on the Croatian War of Independence - fitting, since Srdj also saw some of that war's fiercest fighting. The cable car up is one of the coast's best views.
_facts: 412-metre mountain behind the walled city, part of the Dinaric Alps; popular viewpoint over the Old City, Lokrum and the Adriatic
Fort Imperial, built by the French in 1810 during the Napoleonic Wars, stands at the summit and now houses the Museum of the Croatian War of Independence
City name derives from dubrava (oak grove) which once covered the mountain's slopes; Srdj saw fierce fighting during the 1991-95 Siege of Dubrovnik; cable car reopened after wartime damage

s: The oldest working Sephardic synagogue on Earth
w: Established in 1352 and still in occasional use, this is the oldest Sephardic synagogue anywhere still functioning as one, and the second-oldest synagogue in Europe. The small Jewish community that owns it opens the main floor for the High Holy Days; otherwise it operates as a museum of centuries-old ritual objects.
_facts: Orthodox Jewish synagogue, said to have been established 1352, gaining legal status in the city in 1408
Oldest Sephardic synagogue in use in the world; second-oldest synagogue in Europe
Main floor still used for High Holy Days and special occasions; otherwise operates mainly as a Jewish museum

s: The church of the saint who protected a republic
w: Saint Blaise didn't just watch over Dubrovnik - by tradition he was the personal protector of the entire Republic of Ragusa, and this Baroque church built in his name remains a central landmark. The devotion runs deep enough that Croatia's Ministry of Culture protects it as intangible cultural heritage.
_facts: Catholic Baroque church, one of Dubrovnik's major sights
St Blaise (St Vlaho) is the patron saint of Dubrovnik and formerly protector of the independent Republic of Ragusa
Protected as intangible cultural heritage by Croatia's Ministry of Culture

s: Where the Republic quarantined its arrivals
w: Just outside the walls sits a cluster of stone buildings that once served as Ragusa's quarantine station - travelers and goods held here before being trusted inside the city. An early, practical piece of plague-era public health, built long before germ theory existed, still standing intact by the old harbour.
_facts: Group of interconnected buildings around 300 metres from Dubrovnik's walls
Once used as a quarantine station for the Republic of Ragusa

s: A children's camp, and a mass grave, on one islet
w: A children's holiday camp occupies most of this small Elaphiti islet today - a strange neighbor to its darker history. In May 1945, Partisans executed 204 German and Croatian POWs here. The site lay unmarked until 2013, when exhumations recovered 214 sets of remains, reburied at Dubrovnik's Home Guard cemetery.
_facts: Uninhabited islet in the Elaphiti Islands, northwest of Dubrovnik; a children's resort and recreational centre is located on it
Site of a mass execution of 204 German and Croatian prisoners of war by Yugoslav Partisans in May 1945
Exhumation began mid-February 2013; remains of 214 males recovered, buried in a joint grave at Dubrovnik's Home Guard cemetery on 1 March 2013

s: The one Old Town palace the 1667 quake spared
w: When the 1667 earthquake flattened much of Dubrovnik, this palace came through untouched - as if its honest-weights inscription had earned it protection. Built in the 1520s, it served in turn as customs house, mint, armoury and bank. Today it holds the Republic's own archive, with documents dating from 1022.
_facts: 16th-century Gothic-Renaissance palace, built 1516-1522; also called Divona
Survived the 1667 earthquake without damage; served over time as customs office, mint, armoury, treasury, bank and school
Now home to the Dubrovnik State Archive, with documents from as early as 1022 and more than 7,000 volumes of manuscripts

s: A monastery with its own working pharmacy
w: Right on the Stradun, Dubrovnik's main artery, this Franciscan complex packs a church, a library and a pharmacy behind one facade - a self-contained world a medieval monastery was built to be. The old pharmacy has kept dispensing remedies for centuries, one of the enduring curiosities along the city's busiest street.
_facts: Large complex belonging to the Order of the Friars Minor: friary, church, library and pharmacy
Situated on the Placa (Stradun), Dubrovnik's main street

s: A small votive chapel on the Stradun
w: Tucked beside its much larger Franciscan neighbor on the Stradun, this small votive church is easy to walk past and just as easy to miss the point of: built as an offering, dedicated to Christ, rather than for any parish. A modest, quiet counterpoint to the grander architecture crowding the street around it.
_facts: Small votive church in Dubrovnik's Old Town, dedicated to Jesus Christ
Located beside the Franciscan friary complex

s: The 31-metre marker at the end of the Stradun
w: Standing 31 metres over Luza Square at the far end of the Stradun, this bell tower has marked the meeting point of Dubrovnik's Old Town for centuries - the spot where the city's main street runs out and its public life has always gathered, from state ceremonies to the daily passeggiata.
_facts: Tower on Luza Square at the end of the Stradun, 31 metres high
